title: Structural Engineering
summary: Load-path analysis, seismic detailing and frame design that let architecture reach further on less material.
lede: Every scheme starts with the load path. Get that right and the rest of the building gets cheaper, lighter and easier to build.
body: We size and detail frames in steel, concrete and timber, from single-storey portal sheds to forty-storey towers. Analysis runs in the same model the drawings come out of, so a change to a member size is a change everywhere it appears.

Assessment work is a large part of what we do. Owners come to us with a structure that has to carry more than it was built for, and the answer is usually a targeted strengthening scheme rather than a replacement.

title: Civil and Infrastructure
summary: Roads, bridges, drainage and site works engineered for a hundred year horizon and a changing climate.
lede: Ground is the least forgiving part of any project. We survey it, model it, and design what sits on it.
body: Our civil team takes a site from topographic survey through earthworks, drainage and pavement design to the point where a contractor can price it without a list of assumptions.

Flood and stormwater work is modelled against the rainfall the site will see in fifty years, not the rainfall it saw last year. That changes attenuation volumes, and it is cheaper to find out at design stage.

title: Mechanical and Process
summary: Piping, thermal systems and plant layouts tuned for throughput, redundancy and quiet operation.
lede: Process plant lives or dies on layout. Pipe runs, access and maintenance decide the operating cost for the next thirty years.
body: We design piping systems and their supports, run stress analysis on hot lines, and lay out plant so that the units needing weekly attention are the ones a fitter can reach.
Energy work is measured, not assumed. We meter the existing plant first, then model the change, so the saving in the report is the saving on the bill.
deliverables: P and ID and line lists

title: Digital Engineering
summary: One coordinated model that every discipline works from, and that survives into operation.
lede: A model is worth having when the site team opens it. Everything else is a picture of a building.
body: We run federated models across structure, civils, mechanical and electrical, with a clash routine that closes issues rather than counting them.
Parametric work pays for itself on repetitive geometry: a node family that resolves itself against member sizes saves weeks of drafting on a diagrid or a long viaduct.

title: Steel Fabrication and Erection
summary: Connection design, shop detailing and erection sequencing, from the drawing office to the last bolt.
lede: Steel is decided in the connections. Design them early and the frame goes up in the order the crane wants.
body: We detail connections to the fabricator's shop standards rather than a generic library, which cuts weld volume and keeps the pieces inside the transport envelope.
Erection sequence is designed alongside the frame, with the temporary stability case checked at every stage, so nothing on site waits on a stability check that was never done.

title: Groundworks and Foundations
summary: Piling, rafts and retaining structures designed against the ground that is actually there.
lede: The cheapest foundation is the one that matches the ground investigation, not the one that matches the last job.
body: We specify and interpret ground investigation, then design the foundation that suits it, whether that is a raft on improved ground or bored piles to rock.
Settlement is checked against the structure above, because a slab that moves within tolerance still cracks a facade that does not.

title: Industrial Plant Construction
summary: Full delivery of process and energy plant, from foundations to the day it runs.
lede: Building next to a plant that is still running is a different job from building on an empty field.
body: We take plant projects from foundations through structures, pipework and electrical to a working handover, holding the interfaces between packages so the client is not left arbitrating them.
Tie-ins to live systems are planned around the shutdown window that actually exists, and rehearsed before it opens.

title: Commissioning and Handover
summary: Proving the thing works, and leaving the operator with records they can use.
lede: A project ends when the operator can run it without ringing us, not when the last valve is fitted.
body: Commissioning is planned from the design stage, so the instrumentation needed to prove performance is in the drawings rather than added later.
Handover includes the as-built model, the test records and time with the people who will operate it. Most of the value of a digital model is realised after practical completion.
